name: Anger & Irritation
description: Recurrent patterns of anger outbursts, persistent irritability, or difficulty managing frustration that feels out of proportion to situations, affecting relationships and daily functioning.

immediateActions.title: 60-Second Cool Down
instructions: As soon as you notice anger rising, say silently to yourself: I am feeling angry and I have space to choose my response
Step back physically if possible: take one step away or turn slightly
Take a fast, deep inhale through the nose for 2 counts, then exhale slowly through pursed lips for 6 counts
Repeat the breath pattern 3 more times
Ask yourself: On a scale of 1-10, how hot is my anger right now? Name it aloud if safe
Ask: What do I actually need right now? Space? A drink? To say nothing for 2 minutes?

immediateActions.title: 90-Second Timeout Protocol
instructions: As soon as you feel irritation rising, say silently: I need 90 seconds
If in a conversation, say gently: I need a moment, I will come back in 2 minutes
Physically remove yourself to a quiet space if possible
Splash cold water on your face or hold a cold object
Breathe in for 4 counts, hold 4, exhale 6 — repeat 5 times
Ask yourself: What am I really feeling underneath? Hurt? Fear? Disrespected? Tired?
Wait until you can name the secondary feeling before returning

immediateActions.title: Physical Release Sequence
instructions: Go somewhere private if possible
Clench your fists as tightly as you can for 5 full seconds, then release completely and shake out your hands
Tense all the muscles in your face, hold for 5, then release and sigh out loud
Push both hands against a wall as hard as you safely can for 5 seconds, then release
March or jog in place vigorously for 30 seconds, then stop and stand still
Take 3 slow breaths in and out and notice the shift in energy

immediateActions.title: Heat Mapping: Body Scan for Anger
instructions: Close your eyes and mentally scan your body from head to toe
Notice where the anger lives: tight jaw? Clenched fists? Tight chest? Hot face?
Rate the heat/intensity from 1 to 10 in each body area
For the hottest area, breathe INTO it for 3 breaths: imagine cool air flowing in, tension melting out
Clench and release each tight muscle group on each exhale
After releasing, re-rate the intensity and notice the difference

immediateActions.title: Anger Unpacking: What Is Underneath?
instructions: Write the event that triggered your anger in one or two sentences
Rate the anger from 1 to 10
Ask: Under the anger, am I also feeling hurt? Unheard? Disappointed? Afraid? Overwhelmed? Disrespected?
Circle any secondary feelings that are also present
Ask: What is it that I wanted or needed in this situation that I did not get?
Write down one thing you want to say or do next, and one thing you want to avoid saying or doing

immediateActions.title: Perspective Shift: 3 Angles
instructions: Write the triggering event in 1 sentence
Angle 1 — My view: Write your perspective, your feelings, your assumptions
Angle 2 — Their view: Write what might the other person (or situation) be experiencing? Be generous in imagining
Angle 3 — Observer view: What would a neutral, wise friend say about this?
After writing all 3, ask: Is my original interpretation the only possible one?
Choose one response that would move things forward productively

immediateActions.title: Constructive Expression Prompt
instructions: Decide what the actual issue is, separate from the person involved
Write one sentence using the I-statement format: I feel [emotion] when [specific situation/action] because [effect on you]
Write down one specific request of what you would like instead, framed positively
Choose a good time to speak: not when either of you is hungry, tired, or still heated
Deliver your I-statement calmly and state your request clearly
Listen to the response without interrupting; you do not have to agree, just to hear

safetyGuidance: Anger is a natural human emotion that signals something matters to us — the goal is not to eliminate it, but to express it in ways that do not harm yourself or others. Anger issues are treatable and often stem from unmet needs, past experiences, or current stressors. If anger is causing harm to yourself or your relationships, working with a therapist (especially one trained in CBT or DBT) can help you build lasting regulation skills. If you ever feel at risk of harming yourself or someone else, please reach out to emergency services or a crisis line immediately.
